title: Statistical-query complexity of sparse halfspaces
formal: Do there exist absolute constants \(C\ge 2\) and \(a,b>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge 2\) and \(1\le r\le n, SQ-DIM(Hn,r, 1/[C(r \log _{2} n)^{a}])\le C n^{b}\), where Hn,r is the class of r-sparse halfspaces on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and SQ-DIM is the distribution-worst-case correlation parameter defined below?
why: Clarifies whether a statistical-query learner can exploit sparsity while tolerating coarse, sample-efficient estimates. The problem isolates an informational obstruction from the cost of reading many irrelevant coordinates, without assuming a favorable data distribution.
status_note: Source Problem 3 and its definitions checked, with subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026. No resolution of this worst-distribution, inverse-\(\operatorname{poly}(r \log  n)\) parameter question was located. Results for noisy, Gaussian, smoothed or ordinary sample-access learning do not automatically settle it. No exhaustive literature or proof audit is claimed.

progress.text: Feldman states the precise sparse-halfspace correlation-dimension question and connects the parameter to attribute-efficient SQ learning.

sentences: An r-sparse halfspace uses at most r of the n Boolean input coordinates.
Statistical-query learning accesses approximate expectations instead of individual labeled examples.
The source asks whether the worst-case number of nearly uncorrelated sparse halfspaces stays polynomial in n when correlation is inverse-polynomial in r log n.
Both the sparsity dependence and the worst-case distribution are essential to the question.
A resolution would clarify the informational limits of exploiting sparse structure through statistical queries.

upgraded_from.title: The Statistical Query Complexity of Learning Sparse Halfspaces

definitions: A member of Hn,r is a function \(h:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{- 1,+1\}\) of the form \(h(x)=+1\) if \(\sum j w_{j}x_{j}\ge \theta\) and \(h(x)=- 1\) otherwise, where \(w\in \mathbb{R} ^{n}\) has at most r nonzero coordinates and \(\theta \in \mathbb{R}\). Different weight representations of the same function define one member. For any probability distribution D on the finite cube and \(0<\gamma <1, SQ-DIM(Hn,r,D,\gamma )\) is the largest integer d for which there are d distinct functions \(h_{1},\ldots ,hd\) in Hn,r satisfying |\(\sum x D(x)h_{i}(x)h_{j}(x)|\le \gamma\) whenever \(i\ne j\). Then \(SQ-DIM(Hn,r,\gamma )\) is the maximum of this integer over all D, without any uniformity, product-distribution or margin promise. These maxima exist because the Boolean function class is finite and each feasible correlation condition is a closed constraint on the finite probability simplex. The constants C,a,b must work simultaneously for all n,r and all distributions. This is exactly the polynomial-versus-superpolynomial parameter question in source Problem 3, with its \(O(1)\) exponents made explicit. It asks for an upper bound on this dimension, not polynomial time to enumerate the functions or evaluate real weights.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed universal polynomial bound for some fixed C,a,b, or prove its negation: for every choice of such constants there are n,r and a distribution supporting a family larger than \(Cn^{b}\) with pairwise absolute correlations at most \(1/[C(r \log _{2} n)^{a}]\). The target is this source-defined parameter statement, not a guarantee restricted to one distribution or to halfspaces with large margin.

context_blocks.title: Learning with many irrelevant coordinates
context_blocks.text: A sparse halfspace uses at most r of n coordinates, even though the learner does not know which ones matter. For example, a rule depending only on \(x_{7}\) is one-sparse regardless of how many other features are supplied. Attribute efficiency asks whether learning can benefit from this sparsity without requiring labeled information proportional to every coordinate.

context_blocks.title: What a statistical query reveals
context_blocks.text: An SQ learner asks for an approximate expectation of a bounded function \(\varphi (x,h(x))\in [- 1,1]\). A tolerance \(\tau\) allows any answer within \(\tau\) of the true expectation. Smaller tolerance requires more precise information. The source relates inverse-polynomial tolerance in r log n to attribute-efficient use of labeled examples.

context_blocks.title: Why nearly uncorrelated functions appear
context_blocks.text: Under the uniform distribution, the one-sparse rules \(2x_{1}- 1\) and \(2x_{2}- 1\) have correlation zero: they agree as often as they disagree. SQ-DIM asks how many candidate halfspaces can be almost uncorrelated at once under the same distribution. It then takes the worst distribution, which need not be uniform.

context_blocks.title: The two polynomial requirements differ
context_blocks.text: The allowed correlation scale is inverse-polynomial in r log n, while the required bound on the number of nearly uncorrelated functions is polynomial in n. Replacing the latter with a polynomial in r log n would ask for a stronger statement. Allowing inverse-polynomial tolerance in n instead would change the intended attribute-efficiency regime.

context_blocks.title: What the source result establishes
context_blocks.text: The source gives bounds connecting this correlation parameter to weak SQ learning. Its discussion of converting weak learning to high accuracy additionally allows unlabeled samples. The exact Problem 3 dimension question keeps those access models distinct.
